extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, patent attorneys, rights-holders and applicants in the Philippines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on registration, fees, timelines, third-party participation, assignment/licensing, enforcement, and remedies for patents, utility models, industrial designs, trademarks, geographical indications and copyrights in the Philippines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright registration process
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant shall file the application, which may either be a single or bulk registration. IPOPHL shall review the work for proper categorization, completeness of the documents, correctness and consistency of the registration. Upon finding that the copyright registration documents are in order, IPOPHL shall issue a statement of account, and the applicant shall pay the necessary fees. Finally, after IPOPHL encodes, scans, and upload the application, a Certificate of Registration would be released to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may be author, heir or assignee. Certificate of Registration shall be released to the applicant within seven (7) working days from filing of the copyright registration with complete documents. Copyright registration is not mandatory for protection but may be deposited for evidentiary purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication registration procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant shall file an application with IPOPHL, including details of the applicant, geographical indication, applicable goods, description of geographical area, specifications, certification from government agency, and evidence of its link to the specific geographical origin. IPOPHL shall examine the application to ensure compliance with legal requirements and distinctiveness. IPOPHL shall release a Registrability Report, if any. The deficiency in the application shall be remedied within two (2) months from mailing date of notice. It will then publish the registered mark for three (3) months in the IPOPHL E-Gazette, with corresponding payment of publication fee. If there is no opposition, IPOPHL shall register the geographical indications for protection against unauthorized use of the geographical indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required contents and remedy period (2 months) are specified; publication for 3 months in IPOPHL E-Gazette; registrability report may issue prior to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent registration timeline and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Registering a patent in the Philippines is generally a longer process as compared to the other registered IP rights, taking from three (3) to five (5) years. The patent’s term shall be twenty (20) years from the filing date, subject to payment of annual fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Period variance accounts for responses to office actions and amendments. Annual fees must be paid from the 4th anniversary onward to maintain validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility models, industrial designs and layout-designs timeline and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration process may take at least six (6) months to a year. Grant of registration for a utility model is seven (7) years without possibility of renewal. Industrial and layout-design are initially valid for five (5) years from the filing date and may be renewed for not more than two (2) consecutive periods of five (5) years each by paying a renewal fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee should be paid within a year of the expiration of the registration. Timelines and renewal structure differ by right (utility model non-renewable; designs renewable twice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark timeline and term
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire trademark application may take at least six (6) months to one (1) year. Upon publication and payment of fees, the certificate of registration of the trademark shall remain in force for 10 years and may be renewed for another ten (10) years upon expiration and upon payment of the prescribed fees as per the IP Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and payment are prerequisites to issuance. Renewal process and fees are prescribed; failure to comply with post-registration requirements (e.g., DAU) may affect registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications timeline and term (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire Geographical Indication registration process may take six (6) months up to a year. A registered Geographical Indication shall be protected for an unlimited term, unless revoked with finality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GI registration is perpetual; revocation possible by final action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright protection term and certificate timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire copyright registration process would usually take several weeks to a few months, depending on volume of the copyright creation. The Certificate of Registration shall be released to the applicant within seven (7) working days from filing of the copyright registration with complete documents. Copyright economic rights shall be protected during the lifetime of the author, and for fifty (50) years after his death. In case of works of joint authorship, protection is for the life of the last surviving author and for fifty (50) years after his death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration not required for protection but useful as evidentiary deposit; timelines depend on volume and completeness of filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party observations for patents after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: After the publication of a patent application, any interested party may present observations in writing concerning the patentability of the invention which shall be communicated to the applicant who may comment on them. Thereafter, a conference may be requested to obtain a better understanding of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties can formally challenge or comment; process allows applicant response and possible conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to withdrawal for utility models/designs/layouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Within fifteen (15) days from the date of publication of the declaration of withdrawal, any person who believes that he or she will be prejudiced by the withdrawal of the registration may present a written Opposition to the withdrawal, with payment of fees. The Opposition shall be in the form of a sworn statement stating the personal information and circumstance of the affiant and the reasons why he or she shall be prejudiced by the voluntary withdrawal. The sworn statement shall be substantiated by evidence or proof. The IPOPHL shall notify the petitioner of such opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict 15-day window; opposition requires sworn statement and supporting evidence; fees apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark opposition after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the application is published in the IPOPHL Official Gazette, the 30-day publication period gives any party who may be damaged or prejudiced by the registration of trademark may file an opposition with the IPOPHL through the Bureau of Legal Affairs. The opposition proceeding is an Inter Partes case which means 'between or among parties' and is governed by the Rules on Inter Parties Proceedings. Thereafter, the Bureau of Legal Affairs shall serve a notice of the filing of opposition and the date of hearing to the applicant and the oppositor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 30-day opposition period; opposition proceedings are inter partes and follow defined procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party observation for geographical indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Within one (1) month from the publication of the application of the geographical indication and upon payment of the prescribed fee, any interested person who may be damaged by its registration may file before the Bureau Director of Trademark, as the registrar, a Notice of Third-Party Observation with regard to the registrability of the geographical indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1-month window from publication; fee required to file the observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure for refused patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The final order of refusal of the examiner to grant the patent may be reversed through a petition or appeal to the Bureau Director of Patents within a non-extendible period of two (2) months from the mailing date. Thereafter, if the Director likewise denies the application, that decision is appealable to the Director General of the IPOPHL within one (1) month from receipt of the Director’s decision. The decision of the Director General rejecting the application may then be appealed to the Court of Appeals, and ultimately to the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict short deadlines (2 months to Bureau Director, then 1 month to Director General) and further judicial review available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutatis mutandis application of patent appeals to utility models/designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Patent IRR, the appeal process of patent shall apply mutatis mutandis to the utility models, industrial design and lay-out design (topography).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same appeal timeframes/process apply to utility models and designs unless otherwise specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure for trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision of the examiner to deny or refuse the registration or renewal of a trademark may be reviewed by the Bureau Director of Trademark by filing a petition or notice of appeal within two (2) months from the mailing date of action. The aggrieved party may further contest the adverse decision of the Director by filing a motion for reconsideration with the Director or by appealing to the Director General, within thirty (30) days from receipt thereof. If the appeal is unsuccessful, a party may seek judicial review before the Court of Appeals by filing an appeal within fifteen (15) days from receipt thereof, and ultimately with the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple administrative remedies with specific short deadlines (2 months, 30 days, 15 days) before judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent filing fee requirement at filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application shall be subject to the full payment of the filing fee and the publication fee (1st publication) upon filing of the application, otherwise it shall be deemed as failed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pay required fees in full on filing causes application to be deemed failed. Current basic application fee: Php 2,000.00 for small entities (≤P100M assets) or Php 4,320.00 for big entities (>P100M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent annual maintenance fees and schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: After four (4) years from the application’s publication, and on each subsequent anniversary of that date, the applicant must pay an annual fee to maintain the registration. The patent’s terms are valid for twenty (20) years from the date of filing, with no possibility of renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual fees required from year 4 to year 20; failure to pay leads to lapse (see consequences). A table of year-by-year fees is provided in the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model/industrial design/layout filing and publication fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications for utility model, industrial design and lay-out design shall be subject to the full payment of the following upon application: (a) Filing Fees of Php1,720.00 for small entities and Php3,600 for big entities; and (b) Publication Fees of Php920.00 for small entities and Php960 for big entities. Failure to pay all required fees in full upon filing an application will result in the application being considered a failed one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant can retrieve a failed application by filing a formal written request within four (4) months from the date of the failure notice; otherwise the office will expunge and dispose of a failed application without publishing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval of failed utility/design application
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant can retrieve such an application by filing a formal written request within four (4) months from the date of the failure notice. If a four-month period passes without filing the necessary request, the office will expunge and dispose of a failed application without publishing it in the IPOPHL E-Gazette. Thereafter, the only remedy for the applicant is to file anew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict 4-month retrieval window; failure to act leads to expungement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model and design renewal fees and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility model registration is valid for seven (7) years and is not subject to renewal. Industrial design and layout design are valid for five (5) years and extendable: (a) first extension term of five (5) years with a fee of Php1,030.00 for small entities and Php2,160.00 for big entities; and (b) a second extension term of five (5) years with a fee of Php2,000.00 for small entities and Php4,320.00 for big entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different fee schedule per extension; utility models non-renewable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark fee structure per class and DAU requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing fees for trademark registration are tiered based on the number of classes. Current fee structure: (a) Php1,200.00 filing fee per class for a small entity and Php900.00 fee for allowance/publication for opposition; and (b) Php2,592.00 filing fee per class for a big entity and Php960.00 fee for allowance/publication for opposition. The applicant or registrant is also required to file a Declaration of Actual Use (DAU) within the third, fifth and tenth (renewal) years from the filing date of the application. Otherwise, the director will remove the mark from the register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DAU filing triggers additional fees: 3rd DAU Php900 small/Php1,920 big; 5th DAU Php1,100 small/Php2,400 big; 10th year renewal DAU Php1,100 small/Php2,400 big.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark renewal fees and surcharges
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewal of registration fee per class shall be Php3,100.00 for small entity and Php6,600.00 for big entity. Should the renewal be done after six (6) months from expiration, there shall be imposed a renewal surcharge fee per class of Php1,500.00 for small entity and Php3,300.00 for big entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late renewal surcharges apply for renewals after 6 months from expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indication fees and perpetual registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Geographical Indication Rules, fees required: (a) basic fee of Php3,000.00 for small entities and Php12,000.00 for big entities; (b) publication fee of registration of Php1,250.00 for small entities and Php2,500.00 for big entities. The registration of geographical indications is perpetual; consequently, there are no renewal fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GI registration is perpetual; distinct fee structure for small vs big entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright deposit and certificate fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Under IP MC 16-012, the basic copyright deposit fees shall be as follows: (a) Php450.00 for small entity and Php625.00 for big entity, with (b) additional fees on issuance of a certificate of deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit is optional for evidentiary purposes; certificate issuance incurs additional fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failure to pay patent annual fees
rubrics_metrics.description: If the annual fee is not paid, the patent application shall be deemed withdrawn, or the patent considered as lapsed from the day following the expiration of the period within which the annual fees were due. A notice that the application is deemed withdrawn or the lapse of a patent for non-payment of any annual fee shall be published in the IPO Gazette and the lapse shall be recorded in the Register of the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grace period of six (6) months shall be granted for the payment of the annual fee, upon payment of the prescribed surcharge for delayed payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to pay industrial design/layout renewal fees
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain the design registration, a renewal fee must be paid within one year before the expiration of the current term, or within the grace period of six (6) months after such expiration, with payment of a surcharge. Failure to pay the renewal fee after the lapse of the grace period shall deem to have the application withdrawn, and cause removal in the registration of IPOPHL. Consequently, the industrial or lay-out design loses the protection conferred by law, particularly the right to prevent third parties from making, selling or importing articles bearing or embodying a design which is a copy, or substantially a copy, of the protected design, when such acts are undertaken for commercial purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely payment or use of grace period with surcharge is essential to preserve rights; removal follows lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failure to pay trademark renewal fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to pay renewal fees shall result to the expiration of trademark registration. Hence, the protection and exclusive rights associated with the trademark will cease. Once a trademark registration lapsed due to non-payment of renewal fees, the owner loses the legal benefits of trademark ownership, such as the right to prevent others from using identical or similar marks in relation to similar goods or services. Further, without a valid registration, the owner cannot enforce trademark rights through legal actions against infringers or counterfeiters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-payment eliminates the statutory advantages of registration and enforcement remedies tied to registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for assignment of patents and related rights
rubrics_metrics.description: To have a binding assignment of a patent to third parties – it must be: (1) in writing and signed by the contracting parties; (2) acknowledged before a notary public or other officer authorized to administer oath or perform notarial acts, and certified under the hand and official seal of the notary or such other officer; and (3) recorded with the IPOPHL upon payment of prescribed fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording is required to give notice and for subsequent dealings; recording process involves submission of original/authenticated deed and duplicate; IPOPHL publishes notice of recording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for assignment of trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: A binding assignment of a trademark registration must be: (1) in writing and signed by the contracting parties; (2) acknowledged before a notary public or other officer authorized to administer oath or perform notarial acts, and certified under the hand and official seal of the notary or such other officer; and (3) recorded with the IPOPHL upon payment of prescribed fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application for registration of a mark may also be assigned and recorded. Upon request and payment, a new certificate will be issued to the assignee for the unexpired period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements and practice for assignment of copyrights
rubrics_metrics.description: To give effect to an assignment, the IP Code provides that it is sufficient to have a written indication of the intention to assign such copyright. However, it is always recommended that the deed of assignment is notarized. If notarized in a foreign country, it must be apostilled or consularized as applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recordation with the Philippine National Library is optional but recommended as notice to third parties and as proof of ownership; recordation triggers publication in the IPO Gazette and return of deed with notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording consequences and timing for patent assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, there is no requirement for the registration of an assignment of a patent. However, if the assignee intends to subsequently assign or mortgage such patent to another person or entity, it is necessary that the prior assignment be registered or recorded with the IPOPHL within three (3) months from the date of the relevant prior assignment agreement or prior to the subsequent purchase or mortgage. The non-recordation of the prior assignment shall render the subsequent assignment or mortgage void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To record: submit original or authenticated copy and signed duplicate; IPOPHL retains duplicate, returns original with notation, and publishes notice in the IPO Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for licensing (Technology Transfer Agreements general requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to be granted with a voluntary license without need for recordation with the DITTB-IPO, the TTA must comply with the following general requirements set out under the IP Code: (1) The governing law of the TTA must be Philippine law, and the venue shall be the proper court in the place where the licensee has its principal office; (2) It must grant continued access to improvements in techniques and processes related to the technology during the period of the TTA; (3) If the TTA provides for arbitration, the Procedure of Arbitration of the Arbitration Law of the Philippines or the Arbitration Rules of UNCITRAL or the Rules of Conciliation and Arbitration of the ICC shall apply, and the venue of arbitration shall be the Philippines or any neutral country; (4) It must require that Philippine taxes on all payments relating to the TTA shall be borne by the licensor; (5) It must allow the licensee to exploit the subject matter of the TTA for the entire duration of the contract; and (6) It must not contain any provision having an adverse effect on competition and trade under Section 87 of the IP Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the TTA meets these requirements it generally need not be recorded to be enforceable against third parties (exception: trademarks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark licensing agreements (TLA) recordation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: TLAs must be submitted to the DITTB-IPO for recordation in order to be enforceable against third parties; they must be notarized, authenticated or apostilled as applicable, and signed by the applicant, registrant, or the assignee of record in case of subsequent assignment. Transfers by mergers or other forms of succession may be evidenced by the deed of merger or by any document supporting such transfer. It must contain a provision providing for effective control by the licensor of the quality of the goods or services of the licensee in connection with which the mark is used. A letter request on the intended recordation must be submitted and addressed to the DITTB-IPO Director. The relevant TLA-IPO Form must be submitted which shall include a verified statement from the applicant that the TLA is not subject to any judicial, administrative, or other proceedings; and payment of the requisite recordation fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark license recordation is mandatory for enforceability against third parties; notarization/authentication and quality-control clauses are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordation requirements for TTAs involving copyrights
rubrics_metrics.description: If the TTA involving a copyright does not conform to the general requirements, it must be submitted to the DITTB-IPO for recordation, which shall require the submission of the Copyright Recordation Form and three (3) copies of the notarized license agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-conforming TTAs involving copyright require formal recordation with specific documentary requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordation requirements for TTAs involving patents/utility models/industrial designs
rubrics_metrics.description: If the TTA involving a patent, utility model, or industrial design does not conform to the general requirements, it must be submitted to the DITTB-IPO for recordation, which shall require: (1) It must be in writing and if in a language other than English or Filipino, the document must be accompanied by an English translation; (2) It must be acknowledged before a notary public or other officer authorized to administer oaths and perform other notarial acts, and be certified under the hand and official seal of the said notary or other officer; (3) It must be accompanied by an appointment of a resident agent, if the assignee is not a resident of the Philippines; (4) It must identify the letters patent involved by number and date, name of the patentee, and title of the invention as set forth in the patent; in the case of an application for patent, the application number and the filing date should be stated, giving also the name of the applicant and title of the invention; and (5) It must be accompanied by the required recordation and publication fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of the patent/application is necessary to avoid ambiguity; foreign-language documents require translation; non-resident parties must appoint resident agent for recordation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory license procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A compulsory license may only be issued upon compliance with the procedure set out under the IP Code: (1) Filing of a verified petition in writing stating the statutory grounds upon which compulsory license is sought, the ultimate facts constituting the petitioner’s cause of action, and the relief prayed for; (2) Payment of the filing fee for such petition; (3) Issuance and service of a notice of hearing for the petition by the Director of Legal Affairs; (4) Publication of the notice of hearing in newspaper of general circulation, once a week for three (3) consecutive weeks and once in the IPO Gazette at applicant’s expense; (5) Hearing of the petition; and (6) Decision of the Director of Legal Affairs granting the compulsory license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsory license is an exceptional remedy with formal filing, publication and hearing requirements; applicant bears publication costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to register licences and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of a voluntary license, if the TTA complies with the general requirements discussed above, there is generally no requirement for registration or recordation of the same with the IPOPHL in order to be enforceable against third parties. The exception to this rule is if the TTA involves trademarks. Such TTA must be recorded with the IPOPHL regardless of compliance with the general requirements in order to be enforceable against third parties. An unregistered TTA involving other intellectual property rights, except for trademarks, which does not comply with the general requirements renders it unenforceable against third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recordation exceptions and consequences are specified—non-recordation or non-compliance with general requirements can render the TTA unenforceable vs third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of exclusive vs non-exclusive licensees
rubrics_metrics.description: Republic Act No. 8293 and its implementing rules and regulations do not provide different rights in respect to exclusive and non-exclusive licensees given. Enforcement of the licensed IP shall be governed by the provisions of the contract itself, and supplemented by general law on matters which are not covered or contain any defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract terms determine enforcement rights; statutory law does not create distinct enforcement regimes for exclusive vs non-exclusive licensees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal sanctions for IP infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement can give rise to criminal liability, but the requirements depend on the intellectual property right involved. Under the IP Code, infringement of a copyright or trademark may result in criminal liability. In the case of patents, a criminal action for patent infringement may be instituted against an infringer only if there is already a final court judgment in a civil action against said infringer and the infringer repeated the act of infringement. Revelation of trade secrets may be punished under the Revised Penal Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal actions are initiated by filing a complaint before the Office of the Prosecutor; if prima facie evidence exists, an information is filed with the trial courts. Assistance of NBI and PNP may be secured for search and seizure warrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement options available (civil, administrative, criminal, ADR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aside from criminal prosecution, civil and administrative cases, and applications for injunctive reliefs, search/seizure warrants may also be filed to enforce intellectual property rights. Parties may independently rely on the IP Code and the Civil Code of the Philippines. Court-annexed mediation and judicial dispute resolution are available post pre-trial in a civil action. For remedies against copyright infringement, trademark infringement, and patent infringement, see specified remedies section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple enforcement routes exist; choice depends on facts and remedies sought. Administrative decisions (e.g., BLA) may be faster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and cost of enforcement procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of litigation (civil, administrative, and criminal cases) vary, usually resolved in 1 to 2 years. For administrative cases, a decision from the Bureau of Legal Affairs may be issued within 6 months from the commencement of the case. The filing fee for civil cases depends on the amount of damages sought (generally 2-3% of the damages). For administrative cases, the filing fee ranges from Php3,000.00 to Php20,000.00. There is no filing fee for criminal cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates given are typical durations; actual times can vary. Geographical indication filings by indigenous communities may have filing fee waivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil IPR court procedure under 2020 Revised Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil IPR case is commenced through the filing of a Complaint which must be verified. Within five (5) days from the receipt of the court of the Complaint, summons must be served to the defendant. Thereafter, within 30 calendar days from service of summons, the defendant shall file an Answer. Pre-trial is conducted; if trial is held, hearings shall begin within 60 calendar days from termination of pre-trial and shall be completed not later than 60 calendar days from the date of the initial trial. The plaintiff and defendant shall have a period not exceeding 30 days to present their witnesses on their scheduled date. Parties may be required to submit memoranda/draft decisions within a non-extendible period of 30 days. Thereafter, within 60 calendar days, the court shall render judgment. All decisions and final orders shall be appealable to the Court of Appeals through a petition for review under Rule 43 of the Rules of Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict procedural timing aims for expedited IP trials; judgment may be executory pending appeal unless restrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal IPR procedural basics
rubrics_metrics.description: A criminal IPR case is filed with the appropriate office in the Department of Justice or the Office of the Prosecutor. The proceeding begins with a preliminary investigation. If prosecutors find prima facie evidence, an information will be filed with the trial courts. The judge evaluates the information and may dismiss or issue a warrant. After jurisdiction over the accused, arraignment and pre-trial ensue which shall be terminated within 30 calendar days. On termination of pre-trial, the judge shall refer the parties to mediation on the civil aspect for 30 calendar days. Hearings proceed with each party having 60 calendar days to present evidence-in-chief. The court shall promulgate judgment not later than 60 calendar days from submission. Appeal is taken under Rule 122 of the Rules of Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural timing is condensed; preliminary investigation is a key gatekeeper for criminal prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs procedures to stop import/export of infringing goods
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bureau of Customs maintains a permanent Intellectual Property Rights Division (IPRD) and an IPR Registry where IP holders may record their IPR. The Bureau may conduct random inspections and may issue an Alert or Hold Order upon the request of an IPR Holder/Owner. If upon examination there exists no basis to subject the goods to seizure, the Alert or Hold Order shall be lifted. Otherwise, the matter shall be referred to the Collector of Customs for the issuance of a Warrant of Seizure and Detention against the shipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording IPR with Customs facilitates requests for alerts/holds; Alert/Hold Orders can lead to seizure and detention proceedings if supported by basis on examination.
